title: Ganymedes. Hyacinthus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Orpheus sits amid the grove his singing has drawn to him, in an assembly of beasts and a throng of birds, and tries his strings before beginning his own song: Jupiter on fire for the Phrygian boy Ganymede, turning into the one bird that could carry his thunderbolt and snatching the boy away to pour his nectar with Juno unwilling; then Apollo, who leaves Delphi without its guardian for the Eurotas and Sparta and the boy Hyacinthus, and whose discus rebounds from the hard ground into the boy's face. The god's doctoring fails and he takes the blame on himself; from the shed blood rises a flower brighter than Tyrian purple, with the cry AI AI written on its leaves. Sparta is not ashamed to have borne the boy, and the yearly Hyacinthia come round again in the manner of those before.

advisory.lede: Jupiter burns with desire for the boy Ganymede, takes the shape of a bird and carries him off by force — an abduction whose evident end is rape.
advisory.more: At X.155–161 the king of the gods burns for the Phrygian boy Ganymede, thinks no bird worth turning into except the one that could carry his own thunderbolt, beats the air with wings the poem calls a lie, and snatches the boy away. The seizure takes less than two lines, and nothing that follows it is described except the boy's new work: he mixes the cups and pours Jupiter his nectar, with Juno unwilling. The song has announced its subject at X.152–153 as boys loved by the gods above, so what the desire is is not in doubt, and the force is in the verb abripit, “snatches away.” The second story in this part, Apollo and Hyacinthus, has no force in it: the boy dies when a discus thrown by the god rebounds from the hard ground into his face. Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Tale nemus vates attraxerat inque ferarum
concilio medius turba volucrumque sedebat.
sentences.l: Such a grove the bard had drawn to himself, and in the assembly of wild beasts, in the middle, and in a throng of birds, he was sitting.
sentences.i: Such was the wood the singer had drawn about him, and he sat there in the midst of a gathering of beasts and a throng of birds.
sentences.n: Tale points back to the grove described just before this part opens, and attraxerat says outright that the singer's music drew it. The pluperfect attraxerat sets the scene before the imperfect sedebat holds him in it. vates is the poet as seer, the word for an inspired singer rather than a craftsman. Magnus prints turba, an ablative under the same in as concilio, a second thing he sits amid, and that is what the literal renders; some editions print turbae, which makes the word depend on concilio instead.

sentences.t:
Ut satis impulsas temptavit pollice chordas
et sensit varios, quamvis diversa sonarent,
concordare modos, hoc vocem carmine movit:
sentences.l: When he had sufficiently tried the struck strings with his thumb and had felt that the various modes, though they sounded different, were in concord, he set his voice moving with this song:
sentences.i: When he had tested the plucked strings enough with his thumb and heard that the different modes, unlike as they sounded, agreed, he raised his voice in this song:
sentences.n: Ut with the perfect indicative (temptavit, sensit) is “when,” not “as if.” sensit governs an accusative and infinitive, varios ... modos concordare, “that the modes were in concord”; the adjective varios sits in one line and its noun modos waits until the next, with the concessive clause pushed in between them. quamvis takes the subjunctive sonarent for that concession. impulsas is the participle of impello, the strings driven by the thumb.

sentences.t:
“Ab Iove, Musa parens, (cedunt Iovis omnia regno!)
carmina nostra move!
sentences.l: “From Jupiter, Muse my mother — all things give way to Jupiter's kingship! — move our songs!
sentences.i: “Begin from Jupiter, Muse and mother — everything yields to Jupiter's rule — and set my song going!
sentences.n: Orpheus begins his own song here, and the mark opened at this point is never matched: the two closing marks that do appear, at the end of 196 and at the end of 208, belong to Apollo's speech nested inside the song. Musa parens is a vocative and is both invocation and family: the Muse Calliope is his mother. move is the imperative of moveo, “start, set going.” regno is a dative with cedunt, “yield to.” nostra is the poetic plural for “my”; the literal keeps “our” and the idiomatic reduces it to the singular, as it does each time the plural returns.

sentences.t:
Iovis est mihi saepe potestas
dicta prius:
sentences.l: Jupiter's power has often been told by me before:
sentences.i: I have often sung of Jupiter's power before:
sentences.n: est ... dicta is the perfect passive of dico, with mihi as a dative of agent — a poetic alternative to a with the ablative, “has been spoken by me.” The literal keeps the passive; the idiomatic turns it active, which is what English prefers. The subject potestas closes one line and its participle dicta opens the next.

sentences.t:
cecini plectro graviore Gigantas
sparsaque Phlegraeis victricia fulmina campis:
sentences.l: I sang, with a heavier plectrum, the Giants and the conquering thunderbolts scattered over the Phlegraean plains:
sentences.i: On a heavier string I sang the Giants, and the victorious thunderbolts strewn across the plains of Phlegra:
sentences.n: cecini is the perfect of cano. plectro graviore is an ablative of means and at the same time a claim about register: the plectrum's weight stands for the grandeur of the theme, and it is answered by leviore lyra at line 152. Gigantas is a Greek accusative plural. Phlegraeis ... campis is the ablative of place where, the field where the gods fought the Giants. sparsa ... fulmina is a participle — the bolts already scattered, the battle already over.

sentences.t:
nunc opus est leviore lyra, puerosque canamus
dilectos superis, inconcessisque puellas
ignibus attonitas meruisse libidine poenam.
sentences.l: now there is need of a lighter lyre, and let us sing of boys beloved by the gods above, and that girls, struck senseless by forbidden fires, earned punishment by their lust.
sentences.i: now a lighter lyre is what is wanted: let us sing of boys the gods above have loved, and of girls who, struck senseless by forbidden passion, earned their punishment by their lust.
sentences.n: opus est takes the ablative leviore lyra, “there is need of.” canamus is a hortatory subjunctive governing two things at once: the plain accusative pueros dilectos, and then an accusative and infinitive, puellas ... meruisse poenam, which the literal renders as “that girls ... earned.” superis is a dative of agent with dilectos. inconcessis stands in one line and its noun ignibus opens the next, so the reader meets “forbidden” before learning what is forbidden. meruisse is not neutral — it is “earned, deserved” — and both layers keep that verdict, which is the song's own.

sentences.t:
Rex superum Phrygii quondam Ganymedis amore
arsit, et inventum est aliquid, quod Iuppiter esse,
quam quod erat, mallet.
sentences.l: The king of the gods above once burned with love of Phrygian Ganymede, and something was found which Jupiter would rather be than what he was.
sentences.i: The king of the gods once burned with love for Ganymede of Phrygia, and something was found that Jupiter would sooner be than what he was.
sentences.n: superum is the older genitive plural for superorum, “of the gods above.” amore is an ablative of cause with arsit, “blazed with love,” the standard metaphor for desire. The relative clause has the subjunctive mallet, describing the kind of thing found; esse depends on mallet, with quam quod erat wedged in between the two — “to be, rather than what he was.” Ganymede is called Phrygian because Troy stands in Phrygia.

sentences.t:
Nulla tamen alite verti
dignatur, nisi quae posset sua fulmina ferre.
sentences.l: Yet he does not deign to be turned into any bird except one that could carry his own thunderbolts.
sentences.i: All the same, he thinks no bird worth turning into except the one that could carry his thunderbolts.
sentences.n: dignatur is deponent: passive in form, active in sense, “he deems worthy, he deigns,” and the literal renders it actively. verti, by contrast, is a true passive infinitive, “to be turned,” with nulla alite the ablative of the shape he would take. nisi quae posset is a relative clause of characteristic, subjunctive because it describes a type rather than a known bird. The bird is not named: it is the eagle, the one creature that carries Jupiter's thunderbolt.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, percusso mendacibus aere pennis
abripit Iliaden;
sentences.l: No delay: with the air beaten by lying wings he snatches away the descendant of Ilus;
sentences.i: There was no delay: beating the air with wings that were a lie, he carried off the boy of Ilus' line;
sentences.n: Nec mora is a standing formula with no verb of its own, “and no delay.” percusso ... aere is an ablative absolute, “the air having been struck,” with the instrumental pennis inside it. mendacibus makes the wings themselves the lie: the eagle is the god in disguise. Iliaden is the Greek accusative of a descent-name built on Ilus, the founder of Troy; a name of this shape states descent in general and not a father, which is why the literal keeps “descendant” and not “son,” and why the name says Trojan royalty instead of saying Ganymede. abripit is a historic present, a present used of past action, which puts the snatching in front of the reader as it happens.

sentences.t:
qui nunc quoque pocula miscet
invitaque Iovi nectar Iunone ministrat.
sentences.l: who even now mixes the cups and, with Juno unwilling, serves nectar to Jupiter.
sentences.i: and he to this day mixes the cups and pours Jupiter his nectar, however unwilling Juno is.
sentences.n: qui after the semicolon is a connecting relative, the pattern by which Latin opens a new sentence with a relative pronoun; the literal keeps “who,” the idiomatic breaks it into “and he,” which is what English wants. quoque here is the plain adverb “too, even,” not the ablative quo with -que attached — a distinction worth watching each time the word appears. invita ... Iunone is an ablative absolute wrapped around Iovi nectar inside the line, so the wife's displeasure encloses the service. The presents miscet and ministrat carry the myth forward into the reader's own time.

sentences.t:
Te quoque, Amyclide, posuisset in aethere Phoebus,
tristia si spatium ponendi fata dedissent.
sentences.l: You too, son of Amyclas, Phoebus would have set in the sky, if the grim fates had granted room for the setting.
sentences.i: You too, son of Amyclas, Phoebus would have placed in heaven, if the grim fates had left him room to place you.
sentences.n: The singer turns from narrating to addressing the boy directly — apostrophe — and he returns to it repeatedly in this story. posuisset ... dedissent are pluperfect subjunctives making a condition contrary to fact in the past: the placing did not happen. spatium ponendi is a gerund in the genitive, “room for placing,” with no object expressed; the idiomatic supplies “you,” which English cannot do without. Amyclide is a patronymic vocative, from Amyclas, the Spartan king said to be the boy's father. He goes by several names in this part, and the plain Hyacinthus does not arrive until the discus strikes him.

sentences.t:
Qua licet, aeternus tamen es: quotiensque repellit
ver hiemem piscique aries succedit aquoso,
tu totiens oreris viridique in caespite flores.
sentences.l: So far as is allowed, you are nevertheless eternal: and as often as spring drives winter back and the Ram succeeds the watery Fish, so often do you rise and bloom on the green turf.
sentences.i: In the one way open to you, you are eternal all the same: as often as spring pushes winter back and the Ram follows the watery Fish, so often you rise and flower in the green grass.
sentences.n: Qua licet is “in the way in which it is permitted,” an admission that this is not the gods' kind of immortality. quotiens ... totiens are the correlative pair, “as often ... so often.” pisci ... aquoso is a dative with succedit, split around aries succedit inside the line; the two are signs of the zodiac, and the sun's passage from Pisces into Aries is the spring equinox, so the flower's return is dated by the calendar. oreris is the deponent orior, active in sense, “you rise.” flores is not the noun “flowers” but the second person of floreo, “you bloom” — the addressee is still the boy.

sentences.t:
Te meus ante omnes genitor dilexit, et orbe
in medio positi caruerunt praeside Delphi,
dum deus Eurotan inmunitamque frequentat
Sparten.
sentences.l: You my father loved before all others, and Delphi, set in the middle of the world, lacked its guardian, while the god haunted the Eurotas and unwalled Sparta.
sentences.i: My own father loved you above all others, and Delphi, set at the world's centre, went without its patron while the god spent his time by the Eurotas and in Sparta, the city without walls.
sentences.n: meus genitor is Apollo: the singer is Orpheus, Apollo's son, so the god of this story is his own father, and that is why the telling is so close. Delphi is plural in Latin, which is why positi and caruerunt are plural; caruerunt takes the ablative praeside, “were without their protector.” Delphi lies in the middle of the world because its stone was reckoned the earth's navel. Eurotan and Sparten are Greek accusatives, the Spartan river and the city. inmunitam is “unfortified”: Sparta had no city wall. dum with the present frequentat is “while” inside a past narrative, its ordinary construction.

sentences.t: Nec citharae nec sunt in honore sagittae:
sentences.l: Neither the lyre nor the arrows are in honour:
sentences.i: Neither lyre nor arrows count for anything now:
sentences.n: in honore esse is the idiom “to be held in esteem,” with citharae and sagittae the nominative subjects of sunt. These two are Apollo's emblems, music and archery, and the point of naming them is that the god has set down the things that make him himself.

sentences.t:
inmemor ipse sui non retia ferre recusat,
non tenuisse canes, non per iuga montis iniqui
ire comes, longaque alit adsuetudine flammas.
sentences.l: he himself, forgetful of himself, does not refuse to carry the nets, nor to hold the dogs, nor to go as companion over the ridges of an unkind mountain, and by long habit he feeds the flames.
sentences.i: with no thought for who he is, he does not refuse to carry the nets or hold the hounds or go along as a companion over the ridges of a rough mountain, and long habit feeds the fire in him.
sentences.n: inmemor takes the genitive sui, “forgetful of himself,” and ipse is nominative, pointing at the subject: it is the god himself who has forgotten himself. recusat governs three infinitives, ferre, tenuisse and ire; tenuisse is a perfect infinitive standing in for a present, a poetic licence, and the literal renders it as a plain “to hold.” iniqui of a mountain is “unfair, hard going.” longa ... adsuetudine is an ablative of means wrapped around the verb alit inside the line. flammas is the fire of love, and alit means it is fed rather than lit: the habit is what keeps it burning.

sentences.t:
Iamque fere medius Titan venientis et actae
noctis erat spatioque pari distabat utrimque:
sentences.l: And now Titan was almost midway between the coming night and the night driven away, and stood apart by an equal space on either side:
sentences.i: By now the Sun was almost midway between the night coming on and the night already gone, an equal distance from each:
sentences.n: Titan is the Sun. medius takes the genitives venientis et actae ... noctis, with the pair of participles ending one line and the noun they share opening the next; actae is from ago, the night “driven off,” that is, the one just past. spatio pari is an ablative of measure with distabat. The whole periphrasis says only that it was noon, and its slowness is the point: the narrative dawdles just before the throw.

sentences.t:
corpora veste levant et suco pinguis olivi
splendescunt latique ineunt certamina disci.
sentences.l: they relieve their bodies of clothing and grow bright with the juice of rich olive-oil, and they enter on the contests of the broad discus.
sentences.i: they strip their bodies of clothing, shine with the juice of rich olive oil, and take up the contest of the broad discus.
sentences.n: levant takes an ablative of separation, veste — “relieve of clothing,” which is to say strip. Oiling the body before exercise is the ordinary practice of the wrestling-ground. The three verbs levant, splendescunt and ineunt are presents in a narrative that has been running on imperfects and perfects: the change of tense quickens it, and the narrative keeps moving between the two through these lines. lati ... disci is a genitive singular split around ineunt certamina inside the line.

sentences.t:
Quem prius aerias libratum Phoebus in auras
misit et oppositas disiecit pondere nubes.
sentences.l: And this, first, poised level, Phoebus sent into the airy breezes, and he scattered the opposing clouds with its weight.
sentences.i: Phoebus threw first: he balanced the disc, sent it into the high air, and with its weight broke apart the clouds that stood in its way.
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative picking up the discus from the line before, so the sentence begins where English would say “and this.” prius is “first,” before the boy's turn. libratum is a perfect passive participle agreeing with quem, the discus swung level before release, and the literal keeps it as a participle on the disc. The preposition in stands inside its own phrase, between aerias and auras, an inversion Latin verse allows freely. disiecit pondere nubes is unembarrassed hyperbole: the throw goes through the clouds.

sentences.t:
Reccidit in solidam longo post tempore terram
pondus et exhibuit iunctam cum viribus artem.
sentences.l: It fell back onto the solid earth after a long time — the weight — and displayed skill joined with strength.
sentences.i: Long afterwards the weight came down on the hard ground, and showed a skill matched with strength.
sentences.n: Reccidit is the perfect of recido, “fell back”; its doubled c is the reduplication of cecidi surviving inside the compound, and since the present would be recidit, the doubled letter is what tells you this is the perfect. The verb opens the sentence and its subject pondus is held back to the start of the next line, which is where the weight lands. post stands between longo and tempore, the same inversion as aerias ... in auras at line 178. exhibuit iunctam cum viribus artem is praise of the throw: technique and force together, not force alone.

sentences.t:
Protinus imprudens actusque cupidine lusus
tollere Taenarides orbem properabat.
sentences.l: At once, unforeseeing and driven by eagerness for the game, the Taenarian boy was hurrying to lift the disc.
sentences.i: At once, seeing nothing ahead and carried away by the sport, the boy of Taenarum hurried to pick the disc up.
sentences.n: imprudens is “not seeing ahead,” and it is the word that marks him for what comes. actus is the participle of ago, “driven,” with cupidine lusus, an ablative and a genitive depending on it: “by desire of the game.” Taenarides names him from Taenarum in Laconia — the Spartan boy, and it is the second name the story has given him, after Amyclide. properabat is imperfect: the hurrying is still under way when the ground answers it.

sentences.t:
At illum
dura repercusso subiecit verbere tellus
in vultus, Hyacinthe, tuos.
sentences.l: But it the hard ground threw back up, with a rebounding stroke, into your face, Hyacinthus.
sentences.i: But the hard ground struck it back up, and the rebound drove it into your face, Hyacinthus.
sentences.n: illum is the discus, put first in its clause at the end of one line and left far from its verb subiecit, whose subject dura ... tellus opens and closes the line after. repercusso verbere is an ablative of means with a participle, “with a stroke driven back.” vultus is a poetic plural for the one face. The apostrophe returns at exactly the moment of the blow: Hyacinthe is a vocative, and this is the first time in the story that the boy is called by his own name.

sentences.t:
Expalluit aeque
quam puer ipse deus conlapsosque excipit artus,
sentences.l: The god himself grew as pale as the boy, and catches up the collapsed limbs,
sentences.i: The god turned as pale as the boy did, and he gathers up the limbs as they give way,
sentences.n: aeque ... quam is the correlative pair, “as much ... as”: the god's colour matches the boy's exactly. Expalluit aeque ends one line and the subject deus arrives only in the next, behind quam puer ipse, so the comparison is complete before you are told who is being compared. ipse stands between the two nouns and could be taken with either; it is taken here with deus, the god himself going as pale as the mortal boy, which is how the literal reads it. conlapsos is the edition's unassimilated spelling for collapsos. The perfect expalluit gives way to the present excipit, and the presents run on from here through everything the god tries.

sentences.t:
et modo te refovet, modo tristia vulnera siccat,
nunc animam admotis fugientem sustinet herbis.
sentences.l: and now he warms you back, now he dries the grim wounds, now he holds up, with herbs brought close, the life-breath as it flees.
sentences.i: and now he chafes you warm again, now he staunches the cruel wound, now he holds the fleeing breath in with herbs laid on.
sentences.n: modo ... modo ... nunc sets three remedies in a row, each of them failing. te keeps the address to the boy running through the god's efforts. tristia vulnera is a poetic plural for the single wound, and the idiomatic makes it singular. admotis ... herbis is an ablative of means wrapped around fugientem sustinet, so the herbs enclose in the word order the breath they cannot hold in fact. anima is the breath that is also the life.

sentences.t: Nil prosunt artes: erat inmedicabile vulnus.
sentences.l: The arts avail nothing: the wound was not to be healed.
sentences.i: His skill is of no use: the wound could not be healed.
sentences.n: Nil is an adverbial accusative, “in no way,” with prosunt. artes are Apollo's own, and the line is aimed at that: he is the god of healing, and healing is the thing that fails him. The present prosunt stands beside the imperfect erat — the failure happening now against a wound that had been incurable all along. inmedicabile is a negated -bilis adjective, “not able to be healed,” which is the form the literal shows; it is also the edition's unassimilated spelling for immedicabile.

sentences.t:
Ut siquis violas rigidumve papaver in horto
liliaque infringat fulvis horrentia linguis,
sentences.l: As if someone should break in a garden violets, or the stiff poppy, and lilies bristling with tawny tongues,
sentences.i: As when someone snaps violets in a garden, or a stiff-stemmed poppy, or lilies with their tawny tongues standing stiff in them,
sentences.n: Ut siquis opens a simile whose verbs are all subjunctive — infringat here, then demittant, sustineant and spectent in the two lines that follow — the “if someone should” of an imagined case. The edition prints siquis as one word. The enclitic -ve on rigidum is “or.” The lilies' tongues are their stamens, horrentia meaning standing stiffly out. All three flowers are of the kind that break at the stem, which is what the simile is for.

sentences.t:
marcida demittant subito caput illa vietum
nec se sustineant spectentque cacumine terram:
sentences.l: those flowers, withering, should suddenly let fall their shrivelled head and should not hold themselves up, and should look at the ground with their tip:
sentences.i: and they, going limp, suddenly let the withered head drop, cannot hold themselves up, and stare at the ground with their tips:
sentences.n: marcida is neuter plural agreeing with illa, the flowers; vietum is singular agreeing with caput, because each flower has one head. The line opens with the one word and closes with the other, so the drooping is spread across the whole of it. vietum is “shrivelled, shrunk,” a rare word. cacumine is an ablative of means: the flower looks down by the tip that used to point up. spectent continues the string of subjunctives that the sic of the next line answers.

sentences.t:
sic vultus moriens iacet, et defecta vigore
ipsa sibi est oneri cervix umeroque recumbit.
sentences.l: so his dying face lies, and the neck, its vigour gone, is itself a burden to itself and sinks onto the shoulder.
sentences.i: so the face lies dying, and the neck, its strength gone, is a weight to itself and settles onto the shoulder.
sentences.n: sic answers the ut of the simile and completes it. moriens is a participle agreeing with vultus, “the face, dying.” defecta vigore is a participle with an ablative, “failed as to its strength,” and it ends one line while the noun it belongs to, cervix, waits until the middle of the next. sibi est oneri is the double dative — one dative for the person or thing concerned, one for what it serves as — “is for a burden to itself.” umero attaches to recumbit, “sinks back onto the shoulder.”

sentences.t:
“Laberis, Oebalide, prima fraudate iuventa,”
Phoebus ait “videoque tuum, mea crimina, vulnus.
sentences.l: “You are slipping away, son of Oebalus, cheated of your earliest youth,” says Phoebus, “and I see your wound, my own crime.
sentences.i: “You are slipping away, son of Oebalus, robbed of your first youth,” Phoebus says, “and I see your wound — my guilt.
sentences.n: Laberis is the deponent labor: passive in form, active in meaning, “you slip, you glide away,” the verb used of anything sliding out of reach. Oebalide is another patronymic vocative, from Oebalus, a king of Sparta. fraudate is the vocative of a perfect participle, spoken to the boy, with the ablative iuventa naming what he is cheated of. mea crimina stands in apposition to vulnus and is a plural for a singular: the wound is the god's own guilt, and he says that before he says anything else. The speech opened here is not finished at the end of this unit.

sentences.t:
Tu dolor es facinusque meum: mea dextera leto
inscribenda tuo est! Ego sum tibi funeris auctor.
sentences.l: You are grief and my crime: my right hand is to be inscribed upon your death! I am to you the author of the funeral.
sentences.i: You are my pain and my crime: it is my own right hand that must be written on your death. I am the author of your funeral.
sentences.n: meum is neuter and can agree only with facinus; dolor is masculine and would need meus. The sense does carry the possessive across to both, which is why the idiomatic gives “my pain and my crime” where the literal keeps the single “my.” inscribenda ... est is a gerundive with the verb, the construction of obligation: the hand must be written on the death, as a name is cut on a tomb. leto is a dative with inscribenda, and it ends one line while its adjective tuo comes only in the next, after the gerundive itself. tibi with auctor is a dative of the person concerned, “author of the funeral for you.” The god takes the blame in three sentences running, and the word auctor comes back at line 214 with the opposite thing attached to it.

sentences.t:
Quae mea culpa tamen? Nisi si lusisse vocari
culpa potest, nisi culpa potest et amasse vocari.
sentences.l: Yet what fault of mine is there? Unless to have played can be called a fault, unless a fault it can be also to have loved.
sentences.i: And yet what fault is mine? — unless playing a game can be called a fault, unless loving can be called a fault too.
sentences.n: Quae mea culpa is a question with its verb left out, which is why the literal has to supply “is there.” nisi si is a doubled “unless,” the two words reinforcing each other rather than cancelling. lusisse and amasse are perfect infinitives serving as the subjects of vocari ... potest, “to have played can be called”; amasse is the contracted form of amavisse, one of the edition's older spellings and not an error. The second clause reverses the order of the first — lusisse vocari culpa potest against culpa potest et amasse vocari — so culpa is heard twice within a few words. et here is “also,” not “and.”

sentences.t:
Atque utinam merito vitam tecumque liceret
reddere!
sentences.l: And would that, as I deserve, it were permitted to give back my life along with you!
sentences.i: And how I wish it were allowed me, as I deserve, to give up my own life along with you!
sentences.n: utinam with the imperfect subjunctive liceret is a wish for what is not the case. liceret is impersonal — “it would be permitted” — with reddere as what is permitted and merito, “deservedly,” as an adverb on it. tecum has the preposition -cum attached to the end of the pronoun, the regular order for that word. Magnus prints merito vitam here; some editions print mori vitamque, which makes the wish “to die and to give back my life.” What is wished for is refused by the fatal law in the next sentence.

sentences.t:
Quod quoniam fatali lege tenemur,
semper eris mecum memorique haerebis in ore.
sentences.l: And since by the law of fate we are held, you will always be with me and will cling on my remembering mouth.
sentences.i: But since the law of fate holds us both, you will always be with me: you will stay on my lips, and they will remember.
sentences.n: Quod standing before quoniam is a connecting relative used loosely, “and as to that, since”; the literal takes it simply as “and.” tenemur is first person plural passive, “we are held,” and the plural puts the god under the same law as the boy. haerebis in ore keeps the physical sense of sticking: the name will not leave his mouth. memori transfers the remembering from the man to the mouth itself, which is where the song comes from.

sentences.t: Te lyra pulsa manu, te carmina nostra sonabunt,
sentences.l: You the lyre struck by my hand, you our songs will sound,
sentences.i: You are what the lyre under my hand will sound, you are what my songs will sing,
sentences.n: The two te at the head of their clauses are anaphora, and both are objects: sono is transitive here, “to sound something out,” so the lyre and the songs sound him. lyra pulsa manu is nominative with a participle, “the lyre, struck by the hand,” manu being the ablative of the means of striking; manu itself carries no possessive, and the “my” in the literal is supplied, left by the Latin to be understood. nostra is once more the poetic plural for “my.”

sentences.t: flosque novus scripto gemitus imitabere nostros.
sentences.l: and as a new flower you will imitate our groans by writing.
sentences.i: and as a new flower you will copy my cries of grief in writing.
sentences.n: flos novus stands in apposition to the “you” inside the verb: the boy addressed will himself be the flower. imitabere is the second person future of the deponent imitor, with the older ending -re for -ris; being deponent it is active in sense, “you will imitate.” scripto is an ablative of means, “by writing.” gemitus ... nostros is split around the verb inside the line. The promise made here is kept at lines 215 and 216.

sentences.t:
Tempus et illud erit, quo se fortissimus heros
addat in hunc florem folioque legatur eodem.”
sentences.l: There will be that time too, in which the bravest hero will add himself to this flower and be read on the same leaf.”
sentences.i: There will come a time as well when the bravest of heroes will attach himself to this flower and be read on the same petal.”
sentences.n: et here is “also,” standing second in its clause rather than joining anything. quo se ... addat ... legatur is a relative clause with subjunctives, describing the kind of time meant; English has to render them as plain futures, which is what the literal does. The hero is not named: he is Ajax, whose Greek name Aias begins with the two letters the flower will carry, which is how a second person can be read on one petal. legatur is passive, “be read”; folio is the leaf treated as a page. The prophecy is Apollo's own, and the next line insists that his mouth is a truthful one.

sentences.t: Talia dum vero memorantur Apollinis ore,
sentences.l: While such things were being recounted by the truthful mouth of Apollo,
sentences.i: While Apollo's truth-telling mouth was saying all this,
sentences.n: vero here is the adjective verus in the ablative agreeing with ore, “by a true mouth,” and not the particle vero, “but indeed” — a trap worth watching for whenever the word stands next to a noun that fits it. Apollo is the god of prophecy, so the truthfulness is doing work: what he has just promised will happen. memorantur is passive, and dum with a present is “while” inside a past narrative, which is why the literal puts it into the past.

sentences.t:
ecce cruor, qui fusus humo signaverat herbas,
desinit esse cruor,
sentences.l: look — the blood, which, poured out on the ground, had marked the grasses, ceases to be blood,
sentences.i: look: the blood that had spilt on the ground and stained the grass stops being blood,
sentences.n: ecce is a pointing word, “look,” handing the moment straight to the reader. fusus is the participle of fundo with the ablative humo, “poured on the ground.” signaverat is a pluperfect inside the relative clause: the staining had happened before the moment now being watched. cruor stands at the head of the clause and again at its close, the blood that ceases to be blood, and cruor means specifically blood that has been shed, not the blood inside a body.

sentences.t:
Tyrioque nitentior ostro
flos oritur formamque capit quam lilia, si non
purpureus color his, argenteus esset in illis.
sentences.l: and a flower rises, brighter than Tyrian purple, and takes the form which lilies have, if there were not a purple colour in these, a silver one in those.
sentences.i: and a flower comes up, brighter than the purple of Tyre, shaped as lilies are shaped — except that this one is purple where they are silver-white.
sentences.n: nitentior is a comparative with an ablative of comparison, Tyrio ... ostro, the dye of Tyre that stood for the costliest purple there was. oritur is deponent, active in sense, “rises.” The relative clause formam ... quam lilia has no verb of its own and English has to supply one. si non ... esset is a condition contrary to fact doing the work of an exception: his is the new flowers, illis the lilies, and the only difference between them is colour.

sentences.t: Non satis hoc Phoebo est (is enim fuit auctor honoris):
sentences.l: This is not enough for Phoebus (for he was the author of the honour):
sentences.i: That is not enough for Phoebus, since the honour was his own doing:
sentences.n: satis est takes a dative of the person satisfied, Phoebo, “is enough for.” The parenthesis is the edition's own punctuation, and enim inside it explains why more is possible: the flower is his making, so he may add to it. auctor honoris answers auctor funeris at line 199 — the god who called himself the author of the funeral is now the author of the distinction.

sentences.t:
ipse suos gemitus foliis inscribit, et AI AI
flos habet inscriptum, funestaque littera dicta est.
sentences.l: he himself writes his own groans on the leaves, and the flower has AI AI written on it, and the letter has been called a letter of mourning.
sentences.i: he writes his own cries of grief on the petals himself: the flower carries AI AI inscribed on it, and that letter has been called a letter of mourning.
sentences.n: inscribo takes the surface written on in the dative, foliis, “writes on the leaves.” AI AI is not Latin at all but the Greek cry of grief, ai ai, “alas, alas,” set down as bare letters because the flower's markings are being read as writing; the letters end one line, and inscriptum, in the next, is neuter singular agreeing with them taken as one written thing. The same two letters begin the Greek name of Ajax, Aias, which is how the hero promised at lines 207 and 208 can be read on this same petal: one mark carries the grief and the name together, and neither reading cancels the other. funesta littera is the letter belonging to funerals. Magnus prints dicta est, “has been called,” which is what the literal renders; some editions print ducta est, “has been drawn,” which would make the line about the tracing of the letter rather than its name.

sentences.t:
Nec genuisse pudet Sparten Hyacinthon, honorque
durat in hoc aevi,
sentences.l: Nor does it shame Sparta to have given birth to Hyacinthus, and the honour lasts to this point of time,
sentences.i: And Sparta is not ashamed to have borne Hyacinthus: the honour has lasted to the present day,
sentences.n: pudet is impersonal and takes the accusative of the person who feels the shame, Sparten, with the infinitive genuisse for what causes it — literally “it does not shame Sparta to have borne him.” Sparten and Hyacinthon are both Greek accusatives. in hoc aevi has a partitive genitive after the neuter hoc, “to this much of time,” which is to say to the present. The claim is a civic one: the city owns the story rather than hiding it, which is what prepares the festival in the lines that close this part.

sentences.t:
celebrandaque more priorum
annua praelata redeunt Hyacinthia pompa.
sentences.l: and, to be celebrated in the manner of those before, the yearly Hyacinthia return with a procession borne in front.
sentences.i: and every year the Hyacinthia come round again, kept up in the old way, with the procession going before.
sentences.n: Hyacinthia is a Greek neuter plural, the name of the festival, with annua and celebranda agreeing with it; redeunt is the verb for what comes round on a calendar. celebranda is a gerundive, “to be celebrated,” which marks the observance as something owed rather than merely done. more priorum is an ablative of manner, “by the custom of those who came before.” praelata ... pompa is an ablative with the participle of praefero, the procession carried at the head of the rite. This part closes on a festival that was actually kept, and Orpheus' song runs on past these lines.
